definition: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on AI: the world's first comprehensive legal framework for AI, in force since 1 August 2024 and applicable in stages through 2028.
A machine-based system that operates with autonomy, may adapt after deployment and infers from input how to generate outputs such as predictions, recommendations or decisions (Art. 3(1)).
The core principle of the Regulation: obligations follow the risk an AI system poses. Four levels, prohibited, high, limited and minimal, set the extent of the requirements.

AI practices with unacceptable risk, prohibited under Art. 5, among them social scoring by public authorities, manipulative conduct that harms people and untargeted mass scraping of biometric data. Applicable since 2 February 2025.

An AI system with significant risk to health, safety or fundamental rights under Art. 6 with Annex I or Annex III. Under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (in force since 27 July 2026), the rules apply from 2 December 2027 for standalone Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for systems in products.

Annex III lists the areas in which an AI system is classified as high-risk: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to services, law enforcement, migration and the administration of justice.

Obligations for certain limited-risk AI under Art. 50: people must be able to recognise that they are interacting with AI, and AI-generated or manipulated content, such as deepfakes and generated text, must be disclosed in the cases of Art. 50(4).

The bottom level of the risk pyramid, such as spam filters, warehouse AI or recommendation systems, with no risk-class obligations. Art. 4 on AI literacy applies anyway, as it has since 2 February 2025.
The procedure showing that a high-risk system meets the requirements. The result is an EU declaration of conformity and, as a rule, CE marking before market placement (Art. 43, 47 and 48).
A continuous, documented process across the lifecycle of a high-risk system that identifies, assesses and mitigates risks (Art. 9). Every other high-risk obligation builds on it.
A requirement under Art. 14: high-risk systems must be designed so that people can oversee their operation, understand their outputs, intervene and stop the system when necessary.
A general-purpose AI (GPAI) model that performs a wide range of tasks and can be integrated into downstream systems. Its own obligations under Art. 53 et seq. have applied since 2 August 2025.

The particular risk of very capable GPAI models, presumed above 10^25 FLOP of training compute. It brings tighter obligations such as model evaluations and serious-incident reporting (Art. 51 and 55).

An organisational duty under Art. 4, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744: providers and deployers take context-appropriate measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff and others acting on their behalf. They need not guarantee a particular individual level. Applicable since 2 February 2025.
A machine-readable mark for AI-generated content: providers of generative AI systems mark outputs so they can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated (Art. 50(2)).
AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles real persons, objects or events and would falsely appear authentic. Its artificial origin must be disclosed under Art. 50(4).
A natural or legal person that develops an AI system or GPAI model, or has one developed, and places it on the market under its own name or trademark (Art. 3(3)).
A natural or legal person that uses an AI system under its authority, except in a personal non-professional activity (Art. 3(4)). SMEs are usually deployers, not providers.
The European Commission's Artificial Intelligence Office. It supervises GPAI models, coordinates enforcement across the EU and oversees the GPAI Code of Practice.
Fines for infringements: up to EUR 35 million or 7 percent of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices, lower tiers for other infringements (Art. 99).
A regulatory sandbox under Art. 57 et seq.: a framework supervised by an authority in which innovative AI systems can be tested in real-world conditions before market placement.
The practical link between the GDPR and the AI Act. An organisation that keeps records of processing activities and data protection impact assessments can reuse parts of them for AI governance.
A maintained list of every AI system in use in the organisation, with purpose, risk class and responsible owner. The first step of an AI Act audit.
